name: Facial feminization surgery
lead: Facial feminization surgery (FFS) is a group of reconstructive procedures that move typically masculine facial features toward typically feminine proportions. It is performed mostly for transgender women and other transfeminine people and covers the hairline, forehead and brow ridge, nose, cheeks, upper lip, chin, jaw and the thyroid cartilage (Adam's apple) [1][2]. Because hormone therapy can soften soft tissue but does not change bone, FFS is the route by which skeletal features such as a prominent brow, a wide jaw or a long chin are altered [1]. The visual result described in the surgical literature is a smoother forehead and brow, a smaller and more refined nose, fuller cheeks, a shorter upper lip and a narrower lower face [1][4].

The techniques come from craniofacial, ear-nose-throat and plastic surgery. Douglas Ousterhout, a San Francisco craniofacial surgeon, is credited with developing most of the procedures from 1982, drawing on physical anthropology and measurements of skulls [1][15]. Surgeons plan from CT or MRI imaging, and procedures can be combined in one long operation or staged [1][10]. Wikipedia describes the work as growing worldwide, and reviews describe a continuing evolution in technique [1][13].

Published research is mostly about quality of life and gender dysphoria in transgender patients. A 2016 systematic review by Morrison and colleagues covering 15 articles and 1,121 patients concluded that the surgery appears safe and satisfactory [18], and a prospective international multicenter cohort reported changes in a facial feminization outcome score before and after surgery [3].

In looksmaxxing communities some users look at FFS as a source of techniques, such as brow bone reduction, nose reshaping and cheek work, to change how heavy or masculine a male face looks. Reviews and studies of the operation describe transgender patients only, and surgeons' accounts of what counts as 'feminine' are themselves a topic of editorial discussion [14].

angle.text: FFS physically reshapes bone and soft tissue, so the change in appearance is direct and lasting. Some looksmaxxers discuss borrowing individual procedures, such as brow bone shaping or cheek augmentation, to alter how masculine or heavy a male face looks.

paras: Wikipedia describes male-typical facial bone growth as driven by puberty and notes that hormone therapy can redistribute fat and soften the face but cannot change skeletal features such as the brow ridge, nose size or chin [1]. FFS is described as medically necessary for many people with gender dysphoria, and the Standards of Care of the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH) list certain facial plastic reconstruction among procedures they consider medically necessary [1][16].

Surgeons describe facial gender perception as depending on several areas of the face. Wikipedia reports a 2011 study by Spiegel concluding that the forehead and upper third had more influence on gender perception than the lower jaw or midface, and that one case study placed rhinoplasty among the most influential factors in being perceived as female [1].

Surgeons commonly use CT and MRI to identify features and plan, and procedures are grouped by thirds of the face [1]. Total time under anaesthesia for a full operation can be long, and many patients have several procedures at once [1][10].

The hairline can be lowered or advanced, or restored with grafts. The brow ridge can be shaved down or, where the frontal sinus lies behind it, reshaped and refixed (cranioplasty). A brow lift can reposition the eyebrows, and orbital reconstruction can change eye socket shape [1]. Wikipedia notes that data do not clearly favour one method of ridge reduction over another and that data on orbital work are limited [1].

Rhinoplasty for transfeminine patients reduces nose size and reshapes the tip and bridge; reviewers note it shares its technical basis with rhinoplasty in cisgender patients but is planned around feminine proportions [4][5][6]. A review in Otolaryngologic Clinics lists forehead and supraorbital ridge reduction, cheek augmentation, lip lift, laryngeal chondroplasty, jaw reduction and rhinoplasty as the modifications most frequently sought by transgender women [4]. Cheeks can be built up with implants or fat grafts, and a lip lift shortens the upper lip and can expose more of the upper incisors [1][4].

Chin length can be reduced by shaving or a sliding genioplasty, and the jaw angle and masseter muscle can be reduced; one published technique removes a sagittal section of the mandible from the angle toward the mental nerve region, generally combined with genioplasty [1][7]. Chondrolaryngoplasty, or tracheal shave, reduces the thyroid cartilage prominence while preserving laryngeal function, and reviews describe it as a procedure with rare complications and improved quality of life [8][9].

Reviews of preparation describe patients researching extensively online, medical clearance and, commonly, a supporting letter from a mental health professional [10]. Separate reviews discuss timing of FFS relative to other gender-affirming care and to hair and other treatments [11]. Wikipedia says guidelines should drive the indication and that a second opinion is advised when a practitioner doubts necessity [1].

Access varies. Insurers commonly cover FFS in France, Belgium and the Netherlands, coverage is difficult to obtain in Germany, and in the United States coverage has increased since the Affordable Care Act, with several states requiring it [1]. A study of 660 US gender-affirming surgeons found that 42.7 percent offered facial feminization [18]. Grokipedia reports typical US costs of about $35,000 to $70,000 or more depending on the number of procedures and the surgeon [2].

In 1982 Darrell Pratt, a surgeon performing genital reassignment surgery, asked Douglas Ousterhout to operate on a transgender woman whose face still drew male-gendered reactions. Ousterhout, who had reconstructed faces affected by birth defects and trauma, studied early twentieth-century physical anthropology and cephalometric measurements, and tested his measurements on several hundred skulls [1][15]. He is described as a voluntary clinical professor at UCSF who practised in San Francisco; a 2006 San Francisco Chronicle article called him widely considered the foremost facial feminization surgeon in the United States, and a cited source says he performed nearly 1,700 FFS operations by his retirement in 2014 [15]. The same article reports that only about a dozen surgeons worldwide performed FFS in 2006 [15].

Ousterhout edited Aesthetic Contouring of the Craniofacial Skeleton (1991), and his 2009 guide for transgender women is cited as a foundation of the field [1][15]. He later outlined facial masculinization procedures for trans men in 2011, building on the work of Paul Tessier, and a 2017 case report by Jordan Deschamps-Braly described the first female-to-male facial confirmation surgery [17]. Later reviews describe the field as growing worldwide and still evolving in technique [6][13].

Wikipedia lists risks by procedure: nerve injury (mental nerve damage being the main concern in chin and jaw work), tooth root injury, infection, bone non-union, implant displacement, resorption of grafted fat, impaired nasal valve function, bone-healing problems after forehead work, and vocal cord injury after tracheal shave. It describes overall complication rates as low and notes many can be corrected with further surgery [1][9]. A 2024 study examined soft-tissue complications after FFS bone surgery [12].

Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, reports complication rates between about 5 and 25 percent depending on the study, attributing the spread to uneven reporting, and notes that skeletal change is limited by factors such as cranial size [2]. Morrison's review identified seven complications across the patients it covered [18].

An editorial in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery discusses how surgeons and patients define what counts as feminine in facial planning [14]. Grokipedia raises questions about causal effects on dysphoria and reports research on social perception in which some post-FFS faces were rated as less attractive and more masculine than cisgender female faces; these claims are attributed to that AI-generated source and are contested by clinicians who describe high satisfaction [2][3].

On looksmax.org, posters have asked whether brow bone reduction or other FFS procedures could help men with a heavy brow, and others have discussed what surgery could not change about the midface. Threads on the topic mix serious surgical discussion with disputes over beauty standards and some derogatory language toward trans people, which this article does not reproduce.

A prospective international multicenter study of gender-diverse adults with gender dysphoria compared a facial feminization outcome score before surgery, at one week to one month and after more than six months, alongside photogrammetric measures [3]. A 2016 systematic review by Morrison and colleagues included 15 of 24 identified articles covering 1,121 patients and concluded that FFS appears safe and satisfactory [18]. Wikipedia also cites a 2017 review by Berli and colleagues recommending inclusion in guidelines as medically necessary, and a 2010 study by Ainsworth and Spiegel finding better mental-health quality of life in transgender women who had genital surgery, FFS or both than in those with no surgery [1].

A 2022 systematic review of all peer-reviewed gender-affirming surgery literature screened 15,186 references, found 21 cohort publications on facial feminization among 406 on gender-affirming surgery, and reported that only 4.3 percent of outcome studies used partially validated instruments [18]. Grokipedia reports short-term satisfaction above 80 percent with limited long-term data [2]. No published study has tested these procedures for appearance goals in cisgender men.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, FFS comes up in threads about brow bone reduction, nose reshaping and cheek work for men with a heavy, wide or 'ogre' look, and in debates over whether such changes would make a male face more or less attractive.

claims.claim: Brow bone reduction and similar FFS techniques can soften a heavy male face and make it more attractive.
claims.believers: Some posters argue that reducing a prominent brow ridge could make a man look softer and more 'high trust', and cite film actors with refined features as examples.
claims.experts: Published FFS research concerns outcomes in transgender patients, and surgeons treat brow and forehead work as a major lever on perceived gender; no study has tested the effect on attractiveness in cisgender men [1][3].

claims.claim: FFS cannot fix the midface or fully replicate a female skeleton.
claims.believers: Other posters say a long or large midface limits how feminine a surgically altered face can look.
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports that skeletal change is limited by factors such as cranial dimensions and the face's soft-tissue pattern [2]; surgical reviews list the midface among regions addressed mainly by cheek augmentation and rhinoplasty [4].

claims.claim: A full set of facial implants and reshaping would cost more than limited cheek or jaw work.
claims.believers: Posters compare the cost of multi-site FFS-style work with a single implant.
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports US costs of about $35,000 to $70,000 or more for full procedures; no source compares costs for this use [2].

claims.believers: Patients and clinicians describe improved well-being after surgery.
claims.experts: A prospective multicenter cohort and a systematic review report improved outcome scores and low complication rates, but the evidence base consists mostly of cohorts and case series [1][3][18].

claims.claim: Tracheal shave and jaw reduction carry risks of voice and nerve problems.
claims.believers: Surgeons say such risks are rare with correct technique.
claims.experts: Reviews describe chondrolaryngoplasty as safe with rare complications, while Wikipedia lists vocal cord injury and mental nerve damage as possible risks [1][9].

claims.claim: Hormone therapy and fillers can substitute for FFS.
claims.believers: Some patients use soft-tissue approaches only.
claims.experts: Wikipedia and Grokipedia both say hormones and injectables change soft tissue but not bone [1][2].

card.summary: A set of bone and soft-tissue facial operations developed for transgender women, now eyed by some looksmaxxers for brow, nose and cheek work.
card.note: Evidence is from transgender patient cohorts; use for appearance goals in cisgender men is untested.

quick.overview:
Facial feminization surgery is a group of operations that soften masculine facial features: lowering the hairline, shaving the brow ridge, reshaping the nose, building up cheeks, and reducing the chin, jaw and Adam's apple.

It was developed in the 1980s by Douglas Ousterhout for transgender women. Reviews report improved quality of life and a low complication rate, though the studies are mostly case series. On looksmax.org, a few users discuss borrowing its techniques for male faces.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons plan from CT and MRI imaging and then reshape bone (brow ridge, chin, jaw), soft tissue (nose, lips, brows), and add volume to cheeks with implants or fat. Operations are large and may be staged or combined.
quick.risks: Reported risks include nerve injury, infection, implant displacement, fat resorption, bone-healing problems after forehead work, and vocal changes after tracheal shave. These are major operations under general anaesthesia and costs can be high; coverage depends on country and insurer.
